offence_severity: Minimum: Death (Section 302 IPC), Maximum: Life imprisonment (Section 302 IPC) and 10 years (Section 307 IPC)
physical_harm: One victim died at the spot; another received injuries but survived
number_of_offences: Five offences/counts charged; five were finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the testimony of PW-4 and PW-5, and the nature of the weapons possessed by the accused, which indicated they formed an unlawful assembly with a common object of eliminating the deceased and his brother.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, particularly PW-4 and PW-5, whose testimony was relied upon to establish the case against the accused.
trial_duration: The trial judgment was passed on 07.06.2001 and 12.06.2001 by the Additional Sessions Judge, Bhojpur. The High Court of Judicature at Patna delivered its judgment and order on 03.09.2004. The Supreme Court decision was dated 09.07.2010.
legal_representation: For the Appellants: P.S. Mishra, Tathagat H. Vardhan, Ravi Ch. Prakash, Upendra Mishra, D.K. Jha, D.K. Pandey, Manu Shanker Mishra. For the Respondent: Anuj Prakash, Manish Kumar, Gopal Singh.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused formed an unlawful assembly with a common object to eliminate the deceased and his brother, and that the accused 'RS' fired at the deceased and his brother, resulting in the deceased's death and injuries to the brother. The prosecution also contended that the accused had no right to private defence as they were aggressors.
defence_argument: The defence argued that there was no evidence of a common object among the accused, that the deceased and his brother were aggressors, and that the accused acted in self-defence. They also claimed that the prosecution failed to explain the injuries sustained by appellant 'SJ'.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that an unlawful assembly with a common object can be held vicariously liable for the acts of its members, even if not all members participated in the specific act. The Court also emphasized that the right of private defence is a defensive right and not a right of aggression or reprisal.
precedent_relied_upon: Mizaji & Anr. Vs. State of UP. 1959 Suppl. SCR 940; Masalti Vs. State of UP. 1964 (8) S.C.R. 133; Jai Dev Vs. State of Punjab 1962 SCR 489; Takhaji Hiraji Vs. Thakore Kubersing Chamansing & Ors. 2001 (6) sec 145
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed based on the conviction that all accused were part of an unlawful assembly with a common object to eliminate the deceased and his brother, and that they were aggressors who could not claim self-defence.
